Outer Southern Perth

Vacant since the resignation of Labor's Paul Papalia in July who held the seat and its predecessors since 2007

The by-election will be held on Saturday 29 August

Beachside outer suburban seat in Perth's south between Rockingham and Mandurah

Secret Harbour is home to many young, working families and ranks 4th out of WA's 59 electorates for residents who nominate British or Australian as their ancestry

A safe Labor seat first contested in 2025 and formed largely out of the abolished Labor stronghold of Warnbro

Profile

The outer suburban seat of Secret Harbour sits between Rockingham and Mandurah in Perth's south. The seat is lined by picturesque beaches on its west and also contains large nature reserves in its north and east. As well as Secret Harbour itself the seat is also home to the suburbs of Port Kennedy, Golden Bay, Singleton, and Madora Bay along the coast as well as Lakelands and Karnup to the east of Mandurah Road.

Background

Secret Harbour was first contested at the 2025 state election after its predecessor seat of Warnbro was abolished in a redistribution. With much of Warnbro's territory being placed in Secret Harbor its long-serving Labor MP Paul Papalia transferred to the seat and won it for Labor on a typically strong margin for this part of the state. Papalia was first elected to parliament in 2007 in a by-election for the seat of Peel which itself was later abolished in a redistribution before the 2008 election.

Secret Harbour is one of a string of outer suburban seats along Perth's south coast and the seat's demographics have traditionally been friendly to Labor. The electorate is home to a large number of young, working families, and there are many more people with vocational qualifications rather than a university education. It's a less multicultural seat than the statewide population, and has average incomes despite its high workforce participation.  Those demographics partly explain why One Nation thinks it can have an impact in this by-election. At the 2025 election it was One Nation's eighth-best lower house result and Papalia suffered a 19.8 per cent swing against him, much higher than the 12.5 per cent statewide swing against Labor.

One Nation's state leader, Rod Caddies, has previously claimed his party would be the favourites to win this seat. If the party can win (or come close) in this by-election, it would suggest WA Labor's unchallenged dominance in the state could be coming to an end.

The results of by-elections can be easily overinterpreted, but with the turbulence in political support being observed nationally, this one is also being watched for its federal implications, for both major political parties. How seriously does Labor need to guard its outer suburban strongholds in capital cities across the country? And for the Liberal Party, is the threat from One Nation spreading from regional and rural areas into the cities? Secret Harbour lies largely within the federal seat of Canning, held by Liberal frontbencher and leadership aspirant Andrew Hastie. This is not the strongest part of Canning for Hastie, but the Liberal Party will be watching to see which non-Labor candidate picks up support from disaffected voters.

Tempering expectations for One Nation success are that Labor remains in a solid position in statewide polling (albeit declining from the stratospheric highs of recent years) since last year's state election. At the state level, One Nation continues to trail the Basil Zempilas-led Liberal Party in the limited polling that has been published.

Retiring MP

Papalia was handpicked by former premier Alan Carpenter for the 2007 Peel by-election, which was sparked by the resignation of scandal-plagued minister Norm Marlborough. He joined the Labor party just weeks before the poll and had previously served 26 years in the navy, enlisting at the age of 16. He was twice deployed to Iraq, specialising in the clearing of explosives, and operated a home renovation business after leaving the navy in 2004.

After handily winning Peel in the 2007 by-election the seat was abolished in the leadup to the 2008 state election, at which he ran in the newly created seat of Warnbro in the same area. Upon Labor's landslide victory in 2017 he joined Mark McGowan's first ministry, taking on portfolios including tourism and defence. He became police minister after the 2021 election, a portfolio he held until the troubled rollout of a new firearms regime.

After the 2025 state election, at which Warnbro was abolished and largely reconstituted as Secret Harbour, he became the longest-serving member in the lower house and served as corrective services minister until his resignation. He cited an immediate family member's serious medical diagnosis as the reason for his departure.

2026 candidates · ballot paper order

Tree was born in Subiaco and grew up in Warnbro although she currently lives outside of the district. The 34-year-old worked as an adviser to federal Labor MP Madeleine King, and then moved into a government relations role at oil and gas giant Woodside Energy. Tree says she was motivated to run because of Labor policies like building the Mandurah line, Medicare, and fee-free TAFE. Tree is also a published author, having written a book about her father's life and struggles with addiction.

Herdegen owns multiple Anytime Fitness gym franchises across the southern suburbs of Perth and currently lives in Rockingham, just outside of the electorate. He has previously worked as a personal trainer and won a national weightlifting title in 2023.

Robertson was elected to Rockingham Council in 2025 for Rockingham/Safety Bay ward. Prior to entering politics he served as a submariner in the navy and during his tenure was awarded Submariner of the Year. He currently works in real estate and is also the host of his own podcast, "The Ryan Robertson Show."

Buchanan served on Rockingham Council for two terms until his resignation in April this year, citing a loss of confidence in the council's staff and administrative procedures. Prior to his election to council he served as an advisor to former Legalise Cannabis MLC Aaron Stonehouse and now works for current Legalise Cannabis MLC Brian Walker. He emigrated to Australia in 2003 from the United Kingdom where he served in the naval reserve.

Burdett is active in his local church and has a background in the mining and industrial sectors. He previously stood for the seat at the 2025 state election.

Davies currently works in personal fitness and is also a community organiser. She lists capping rents, cheap and clean energy, and building local housing as priorities for her campaign. She is a defence spouse and links this to her opposition to the AUKUS deal.

Dunne is a lobbyist and has been a member of socialist and communist organisations. He ran in the seat of Nedlands at the 2025 state election and for Midland-Guildford ward in the City of Swan at the 2025 local elections.

Fels was previously a Liberal member of the Legislative Council from 2005 to 2009. After losing preselection ahead of the 2008 state election he recontested his position with Family First but was defeated. Since then he has regularly run in elections, as an independent and with Katter’s Australian Party and the United Australia Party. He says his campaign priorities are upgrading the Kwinana Freeway and ensuring the completion of a new train station in Karnup.

Gullan previously ran as a Legalise Cannabis candidate at the 2025 state election in Collie Preston and the 2025 federal election in Canning. He was disendorsed as the party's candidate for the latter election after it was discovered he had a history of making antisemitic comments.

Howard is the leader of the unregistered Australian Patriots Party who say they adhere to the principles of "national conservatism." He ran in Premier Roger Cook's seat of Kwinana at the 2025 state election, attracting just over three per cent of the primary vote.

Jensen grew up in Cooloongup and Warnbro. He joined the Animal Justice Party in 2017 after witnessing undercover footage from Australian factory farms and slaughterhouses and now serves as Deputy Convenor of the party's Western Australian branch. He has a background in advocacy, policing, research, education, information technology and business. If elected, he says he will strive for stronger animal protection laws, an independent animal welfare regulator, affordable housing, better healthcare and education, stronger manufacturing and trades sectors, and reliable low-cost energy. At the 2025 state election he ran in the seat of Joondalup.

Murrell is aligned with the unregistered Sovereign Australia Party. He is a mechnanical engineer with a history working in the oil and gas industries. Between 2015 and 2023 he ran an alternative living community in Karridale in the south west of the state which was shut down to breaches of local planning laws. He is currently based in Newcastle and says he will run for the seat of Robertson at the next federal election.

Palmer has a background in finance, working as a Certified Practising Accountant. She was also a finance manager in several industries before moving into education, teaching high school maths and business. She has taken leave from her teaching position to contest this by-election. Palmer moved to the electorate from South Australia nearly thirty years ago.

van Lieshout is a former teacher and was a candidate in multiple state and federal elections across the country throughout the 2010s. Her last run for elected office was in 2019 for the Victorian federal seat of Cooper. In 2023 she plead guilty to impersonating a Commonwealth official after importing fake police badges.
